# A lakehouse table inside Postgres

On five million events, a DuckLake copy of a Postgres table answered analytical queries 2 to 9 times
faster than the heap at a quarter of its size, and fetched a single row about a hundred times
slower. The previous chapter got columnar speed by copying rows out of Postgres into Doris.
[pg_ducklake](https://github.com/relytcloud/pg_ducklake) brings the columnar table into Postgres
instead, and one statement makes the copy:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events_lake USING ducklake AS SELECT * FROM events;
```

The table uses the [DuckLake](https://ducklake.select) format. Its rows are Parquet files, and its
catalog of files, statistics and snapshots is ordinary tables in the `ducklake` schema of the same
database. Queries that touch it run in DuckDB, which the extension runs inside the Postgres backend,
so one database can hold row tables for the application and column tables for analytics, and one
query can join them.

## Columns win scans, rows win lookups

The notebook builds the same table twice, as an ordinary heap with a primary key and as a copy made
with `USING ducklake`:

| | heap | DuckLake |
|---|---|---|
| on disk | 301 MB, plus a 107 MB primary key | 78 MB, one Parquet file |
| sum of amount by device | 159 ms | 33 ms |
| daily distinct users | 1,618 ms | 774 ms |
| top ten users by spend | 453 ms | 52 ms |
| one row by id | 0.12 ms | 13 ms |

The three analytical queries read a few columns of every row, which is what Parquet is laid out
for, and DuckDB reads only those columns, compressed, in vectors of 2,048 values. That makes it 2 to
9 times faster than the heap, even with Postgres running the heap scans on two parallel workers.

The last row is the other side of the trade. A lake table has no index, so fetching one row means
skipping the files and row groups whose min/max statistics rule it out and scanning the rest, where
the heap only descends a B-tree. Keep the rows the application reads one at a time in heap tables.

## Writes leave the Parquet in place

Parquet files are never changed in place, so DuckLake keeps small writes out of them. An insert below
a row limit is **inlined** into a Postgres table in the catalog, where queries read it alongside the
Parquet until a flush, or the extension's background worker, writes it out. An update or delete
writes a **delete file** naming the row positions that no longer count. In the notebook, updating
1,000 rows and deleting 1,663 left the 78 MB data file untouched and added a 14 kB delete file and a
19 kB file with the updated rows.

## Snapshots, time travel and a change feed

Every commit is a snapshot in the catalog, with a note of what it changed, and `time_travel` and
`table_changes` read back any snapshot that has not been expired:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM ducklake.time_travel('events_lake'::regclass, 5) t;
SELECT * FROM ducklake.table_changes('events_lake'::regclass, 8, 9);
```

After the update and delete the table had 4,998,337 rows, while its snapshot from before them still
had 5,000,001. `table_changes` returns the rows inserted, updated and deleted between two snapshots,
which is what an incremental job downstream needs.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A rough edge in 1.0.2

`table_changes` over a range that contains a delete fails with `function struct_pack(...) does not
exist`. Afterwards, that connection's DuckDB has lost its catalog until it reconnects, and even
`DROP TABLE` fails. Ranges of inserts work, so the notebook stays on those.
:::

## Partitions help on object storage

`CALL ducklake.set_partition('events_part'::regclass, 'device')` makes later writes split their
files by device, so that a filter on device can skip whole files. On a local disk at this size it
bought nothing, 28 ms for the partitioned table against 30 ms for the single file, because reading
one compressed column of a 78 MB file is already cheap and the row-group statistics inside the file
do part of a partition's job. Partitions pay off on object storage, where a skipped file is a skipped
download, and `ducklake.default_table_path` points the files at S3, GCS, R2 or Azure.

## Joining rows and columns

A lake table joins any Postgres table in plain SQL. DuckDB plans the whole statement and reads the
heap side through its own Postgres scan, as the condensed plan shows:

```text
HASH_JOIN  user_id = user_id
├── DUCKLAKE_SCAN            Table: events_lake   Projections: user_id
└── PGDUCKDB_POSTGRES_SCAN   Table: users         Projections: user_id, pro
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## DuckLake or Doris

pg_ducklake keeps one database and one transaction boundary. The analytical table is written by the
same SQL as everything else and needs no pipeline. Doris is a second system to run, but it scales
out on its own hardware and keeps analytical load off the primary. A Postgres server running DuckDB
queries is still one server, so heavy analytics there compete with the application for CPU and
memory.
:::
